sense: with a past participle: I have seen

evidence: Catull. 9.5: vēnistī. ō mihi nūntiī beātī!
terms.comment: One Latin tense does the work of “I have seen” and “I saw”. Passives and deponents form it with sum: victī sumus, we have been beaten (see be).

terms.gloss: I have been …ing (for a long time)
evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.9.1: jam diū ignōrō quid agās
Ter. Eun. 816: Jam dūdum animus est in patinīs.
terms.comment: What began in the past and still goes on stands in the present, as in French: “my mind has long been on the dishes”.

terms.grammar: habeō with the perfect passive participle agreeing with its object
evidence: Sall. Cat. 58.1: compertum ego habeō (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Fam. 13.17.3: sī nōndum eum satis habēs cognitum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Stresses the state reached. Lewis & Short derives the Romance perfect from it (j’ai vu, ho veduto); in classical Latin it is not yet a tense, and “I have seen” is vīdī.

phrases.english: You’ve come! Oh, happy news for me!

phrases.latin: Quid fēcī? quid commeruī aut peccāvī, pater?
phrases.english: What have I done? What have I deserved, how have I gone wrong, father?
Oh no: I’ve forgotten the name.

phrases.latin: cūr, inquit, turbulentam fēcistī mihi aquam bibentī?
phrases.english: “Why,” he said, “have you muddied the water I’m drinking?”

phrases.latin: Tum pol ego et oleum et operam perdidī.
phrases.english: Then I’ve wasted both my oil and my effort.

phrases.latin: jam diū ignōrō quid agās; nihil enim scrībis
phrases.english: for a long time now I haven’t known how you are; you never write

phrases.latin: Jam dūdum animus est in patinīs.
phrases.english: My mind has been on the dishes for ages.
